options.text: Keep the team small enough to coordinate easily, typically fewer than ten people, and add a second team later if the work outgrows it.
options.rationale: Communication paths grow quickly with team size. A small team can plan and decide together; if more capacity is needed, a second team scales better than a larger first one.

options.text: Staff the team first with the strongest back-end developers, since integration is the riskiest part, and add testers once there is enough to test.
options.rationale: Prioritising the riskiest skill sounds prudent, but adding testers later builds in a handoff and delays feedback on quality. The candidate staffs for a phase sequence the team is not meant to follow.

options.text: Take one representative from each contributing department at around a third of their time, so that every department's interests are represented.
options.rationale: Representation is a governance concern, not a team design. Fractional members split their attention and slow every decision, so the candidate trades the team's flow for departmental visibility.

options.text: Give each developer ownership of one component from the start, so that responsibilities are clear and nobody's work overlaps with anyone else's.
options.rationale: Clear ownership feels efficient, but fixed component owners become bottlenecks and stop the team swarming on priorities. The candidate applies a functional structure inside a team that needs shared ownership.

questions.explanation: An agile team is designed to deliver finished increments on its own, so its composition is judged by whether it holds all the skills the work needs and whether it is small enough to work as one unit. Capacity grows by adding teams, not by enlarging one; dependence on outside groups and fractional members are the costs to minimise when choosing names.
questions.mindset: Compose a team around finishing the work, not around representing the organisation.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is replacing a building society's mortgage-servicing system. Five operations staff are seconded at 60% to run user acceptance tests at the end of each three-week iteration. For the last four working days of every month, their manager takes them back for month-end reconciliations, a regulatory obligation. Twice now, a test window has fallen at month end and the release has slipped. What should you do?

options.text: Ask their manager to shield the secondees from month-end work for the rest of the programme, since the secondment agreement commits 60% of their time to you.
options.rationale: The agreement sets an average, and the reconciliations are a regulatory duty that will win any contest. The candidate fights a fixed, legitimate constraint instead of planning around it.

options.text: Bring in contract testers to run the acceptance tests whenever a test window falls at month end, so that releases no longer depend on the operations team.
options.rationale: Acceptance testing by the people who will use the system is the point of those tests. The candidate substitutes availability for the business knowledge the activity exists to apply.

options.text: Mark the month-end days as unavailable in the testers' resource calendars and arrange the iteration timing so that test windows avoid the end of each month.
options.rationale: The unavailability is predictable and permanent. Recording it in the calendars and planning test windows around it removes the clash at no cost to either the business or the programme.

options.text: Raise the two slipped releases with the steering committee and ask it to decide whether month-end or acceptance testing should take priority in future months.
options.rationale: There is nothing for the committee to decide: the regulatory work takes priority, and the clash can be planned out. The candidate escalates a scheduling problem that sits within the programme's own control.

questions.explanation: A resource calendar should hold every predictable limit on availability, including recurring business obligations as well as leave and holidays. When a constraint is legitimate and fixed, the efficient response is to plan the work around it rather than to contest it or to swap in less suitable people. A clash that happens twice from a known cause is a planning gap, not bad luck.
questions.mindset: Plan around a constraint that will not move instead of fighting it every month.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme developing smart electricity meters, three firmware teams share twelve hardware debug probes that took six weeks to procure. Over the last two iterations, engineers have often spent an hour or more looking for one, and two probes cannot be found at all. Controlling project equipment is within your remit as programme manager, and replacements would take another six weeks. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a sign-out log for the probes with a named custodian and an agreed storage place, and order replacements for the two missing probes now.
options.rationale: This is within your remit and deals with both problems: the log and custodian stop the searching and losses, and ordering now starts the six-week clock on the missing capacity.

options.text: Order twelve further probes so that each team can hold a complete set of its own, which removes the need for engineers to search for a shared one.
options.rationale: Doubling the stock answers a control problem with spending and still leaves probes untracked. The candidate assumes the shortage is one of quantity when the evidence points to how the probes are managed.

options.text: Raise the losses at the next steering committee and ask the programme office to issue an equipment-handling policy that all the teams must follow.
options.rationale: A policy may help later, but equipment control is already your responsibility and the next committee may be weeks away. The candidate escalates a fix that is theirs to make today.

options.text: Divide the probes evenly between the three teams and make each team's scrum master responsible for looking after its own allocation from now on.
options.rationale: Splitting the pool makes accountability clearer but loses the flexibility of sharing, so one team may be short while another's probes sit idle. The candidate trades the pool's value for simpler ownership.

questions.explanation: Shared physical resources need a simple control: a known location, a record of who has each item and a named person accountable. When equipment goes missing, put that control in place within your own authority and start replacing lost items at once if the lead time is long. Buying more or escalating is premature until the control problem is fixed.
questions.mindset: Fix how a shared resource is controlled before buying more of it.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is introducing a new point-of-sale system in 48 shops. The software is built iteratively; the rollout plan, agreed with the retail director, goes live in eight shops a week for six weeks. Each shop needs on-site training, and each of your three trainers can cover two shops a week. Recruiting and preparing new trainers takes six weeks. The retail director's firm requirement is that every shop is live before peak trading begins in week 10. What should you do?

options.text: Have each shop in the first two weeks nominate a super-user who, once trained, helps train staff in a later shop alongside one of the three trainers.
options.rationale: It adds capacity without hiring, but it relies on untested trainers and takes experienced staff out of their own newly live shops. The candidate solves a capacity gap that the date did not require solving.

options.text: Propose to the retail director a revised rollout of six shops a week, which completes all 48 shops in week 8 and still finishes before peak trading begins.
options.rationale: The three trainers support six shops a week, and at that pace the rollout ends in week 8, inside the director's real constraint. Taking the change to the director keeps the decision with the person who agreed the plan.

options.text: Shorten the on-site training and add an online module before go-live, so that each of the three trainers can cover enough shops to hold eight a week.
options.rationale: It keeps the original pace by cutting what each shop receives, which raises the risk of disruption in the shops. The candidate protects a date that had room to move and reduces quality instead.

options.text: Start recruiting two more trainers now and keep the eight-a-week plan, letting a backlog of shops build up until the new trainers arrive to clear it before peak trading.
options.rationale: The new trainers arrive as the original plan was due to end, so shops would go live untrained or late in an unplanned order. The candidate pays to keep a pace the resources cannot support yet.

questions.explanation: When a plan's pace exceeds the resources available, first check what the binding requirement is. If the real constraint leaves room, adjusting the pace to the capacity you have is usually cheaper and safer than adding people with long lead times or reducing what each unit of work receives. A change to an agreed plan still goes to the person who agreed it.
questions.mindset: Fit the pace to the resources when the real deadline allows it.

questions.stem: Your programme for a regional bus operator has finished its predictive design phase. Delivery now moves to three agile software teams, while a predictive workstream installs equipment in the depots. The resource management plan was written for the design phase and assigns named individuals to individual activities week by week. Which two changes should you make to the plan?

options.text: Plan the agile part at team level, with stable membership and capacity per iteration, rather than assigning named people to individual tasks.
options.rationale: Agile teams decide among themselves who does which task. The plan's job for that part is to keep membership stable and capacity known, which is what forecasting depends on.

options.text: Set out how the agile teams request specialists from outside the team, such as depot engineers, including who approves and the lead time.
options.rationale: Shared specialists are where agile teams most often stall. Defining the request route and lead time in the plan makes those dependencies predictable for both sides.

options.text: Remove the agile teams from the resource management plan entirely, since agile teams organise their own work and manage their own resourcing.
options.rationale: Self-organisation covers how work is shared inside the team, not how the team is staffed, funded or supported. The candidate confuses team autonomy with having no resource planning at all.

options.text: Keep the week-by-week named assignments for the agile teams, updating them after each iteration planning session so all workstreams stay consistent.
options.rationale: Consistency of format is not a reason to manage agile teams at task level. The candidate preserves the plan's structure at the cost of the team's self-organisation and creates rework every iteration.

options.text: Move the depot workstream to team-level capacity planning as well, so that the whole programme follows one approach and one set of measures.
options.rationale: Depot installation is predictive work with specific crews tied to scheduled activities, so named assignments still fit it. The candidate applies one approach everywhere instead of tailoring by workstream.

questions.explanation: A resource management plan should be tailored to how each part of the work is delivered. In a hybrid programme that usually means team-level, stable capacity for agile work, named assignments for predictive work, and clear rules for how teams obtain specialists they share. When the delivery approach changes, the plan should change with it rather than being kept or discarded wholesale.
questions.mindset: Tailor the resource plan to each way of working the programme contains.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme replacing a university's student-records system, agile teams build the software while a predictive workstream migrates data, staffed by analysts seconded from the registry. Match each resource decision to the person who should make it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Which developer on an agile team picks up the next story from the iteration backlog.
Whether a seconded registry analyst's migration time drops from full-time to half-time during enrolment week.
Which of two features waiting for the shared data architect's limited time should be worked on first.
Whether to increase the programme budget to hire a second data architect for six months.

options.text: The agile team itself
options.rationale: Agile teams decide among themselves who takes which item. Assigning stories from outside the team undermines the self-organisation that makes its commitments reliable.

options.text: The analyst's line manager in the registry
options.rationale: In a matrix arrangement, the functional manager keeps decisions about a seconded person's availability. The programme supplies the impact; the line manager decides.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: Choosing which feature goes first is an ordering decision about value, and ordering the backlog is the product owner's call even when the constraint is a scarce person's time.

options.text: The programme sponsor
options.rationale: Increasing the budget to buy more capacity is a funding decision, and funding sits with the sponsor. The programme manager can make the case but cannot commit the money.

options.text: The programme manager
options.rationale: Not used. The programme manager coordinates these decisions and makes their impact visible, but each of the four sits with someone else: the team, the line manager, the product owner or the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Resource decisions in a hybrid programme are spread across several owners: teams decide who does what within their own work, functional managers control the availability of people they lend, product owners order work by value and sponsors control funding. The project or programme manager's leverage comes from making impacts visible to each owner, not from taking their decisions.
questions.mindset: Know whose decision each resource question is before acting on it.

questions.stem: Your agile team builds a booking app for a chain of veterinary clinics. Complete each sentence with the way of providing the skill that fits how long the work will need it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Accessibility checks are now needed on almost every story, and nobody on the team can do them, so the team should
The next two iterations carry about three times the usual front-end work, after which the load returns to normal, so the team should
The team's mainframe specialist has had no mainframe work for three iterations, and none remains in the backlog, so the team should

options.text: ask for a person with that skill to join as a full, dedicated team member
options.rationale: A need that appears in nearly every story is permanent work for the team. Making the skill part of the team avoids a standing dependency on outside help for routine items.

options.text: agree a time-boxed loan of a front-end developer from another team, with that team's product owner
options.rationale: A short, known peak is best met with temporary capacity that returns when the peak ends. Agreeing it with the lending team's product owner keeps the cost to their work visible.

options.text: agree his release to work where his skill is needed, with a way to call on him later if required
options.rationale: Keeping a specialist with no work for his skill wastes scarce capacity. Releasing him, with a route back if a need appears, serves the organisation and the person.

options.text: send the whole team on a formal training course in the skill before the work starts
options.rationale: Not used. Training everyone is slow and costly, and it does not fit a permanent gap needing depth, a short peak, or a skill that is no longer needed.

questions.explanation: How a team obtains a skill should follow how long and how often the work needs it. A permanent need belongs inside the team; a short peak is met by temporary capacity that returns afterwards; and a skill that is no longer needed should be released for use elsewhere. Matching the arrangement to the duration of the need avoids both standing dependencies and idle specialists.
questions.mindset: Match how a skill is provided to how long the work needs it.
